verses.text: So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.
Then the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel, the Buzite, of the family of Ram, was kindled against Job. His wrath was kindled because he justified himself rather than God.
Also his wrath was kindled against his three friends, because they had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job.
Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job, because they were elder than he.
When Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men, his wrath was kindled.
Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered, “I am young, and you are very old; Therefore I held back, and didn’t dare show you my opinion.
I said, ‘Days should speak, and multitude of years should teach wisdom.’
But there is a spirit in man, and the breath of the Almighty gives them understanding.
It is not the great who are wise, nor the aged who understand justice.
Therefore I said, ‘Listen to me; I also will show my opinion.’
“Behold, I waited for your words, and I listened for your reasoning, while you searched out what to say.
Yes, I gave you my full attention, but there was no one who convinced Job, or who answered his words, among you.
Beware lest you say, ‘We have found wisdom, God may refute him, not man;’
for he has not directed his words against me; neither will I answer him with your speeches.
“They are amazed. They answer no more. They don’t have a word to say.
Shall I wait, because they don’t speak, because they stand still, and answer no more?
I also will answer my part, and I also will show my opinion.
For I am full of words. The spirit within me constrains me.
Behold, my breast is as wine which has no vent; like new wineskins it is ready to burst.
I will speak, that I may be refreshed. I will open my lips and answer.
Please don’t let me respect any man’s person, neither will I give flattering titles to any man.
For I don’t know how to give flattering titles; or else my Maker would soon take me away.

footnotes.content: Three friends have run out of words. Sometimes we exhaust what we know, yet Job still sits in the ashes. There's a silence that speaks louder than any counsel—a silence that says we've reached the limit of what earthly wisdom can comfort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A young man rises in anger—not at Job's suffering, but at Job's pride. How easy to mistake our own righteousness for God's. When we defend ourselves instead of pointing to the Lord, we have already stumbled into the very trap we accuse others of.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu burns with a double anger—at Job for his self-justification, and at his three friends for their hollow solutions. He sees failure on both sides: the sufferer proud, and the counselors spent. It stings to watch both wisdom and compassion fall short.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Youth waits. Respect for the elder kept Elihu silent while the old men talked. There is honor in listening, even when you sense an error—and a young man shows a kind of dignity when he does not rush to correct his betters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The silence breaks his patience. When the wise voices fall mute, something stirs in the young—urgency, maybe even presumption. He takes their failure as permission, their silence as an invitation to speak what he believes he knows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu names himself clearly—young, aware of his place, yet ready to speak anyway. There is something brave, or reckless, in standing before elders with a conviction burning inside. Many of us never find that courage; some of us mistake it for calling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The old teaching says years bring wisdom. It's a comfort to believe that time heals and teaches us rightly. Yet Elihu challenges even this—what if silence and age have simply made the three friends more comfortable with a lie?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The breath of the Almighty gives them understanding." This is the hinge of Elihu's claim—not age, not experience, but the Spirit itself gifts wisdom. He appeals over the head of custom to the direct work of God. It's a radical move, but also a dangerous one if the Spirit has not truly spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The great, the aged, do not automatically hold wisdom or justice. A young man sees this, and it stirs both hope and presumption—hope that he might have something to offer, presumption that he knows what the Lord sees. We all live in this tension.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Listen to me." Bold words from a young man. He is certain enough of his own vision to demand an ear, certain enough of his thoughts to believe they matter. Pride and conviction live so close together we often cannot tell them apart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He has waited, watched, and listened carefully—a kind of study of the debate. His patience was real, his attention genuine. Yet patience can become judgment; waiting can become smugness. The young man observes and believes himself ready to correct what his elders could not solve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He gave them his full attention, yet none convinced Job. None answered his words. The three have failed, and Elihu has watched them fail. He has marked their weakness and now prepares to prove himself stronger—or so he believes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A warning wrapped in humility. "Don't say we found wisdom and God will refute him, not us." Elihu cautions against the very pride that often attends those who think they hold truth—the pride of standing safely while God does the refuting. Yet he himself walks straight into that trap.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job has not aimed his words at Elihu—the young man hasn't even been in the conversation. Yet he will not answer with borrowed speeches. He promises something fresh, something of his own. It's the confidence of untested youth, not yet humbled by how easily the best words can miss their mark.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amazed silence. The three friends stand frozen, voiceless. Elihu reads this as an opening, as permission. But sometimes silence is not an invitation—sometimes it is simply exhaustion, or a sign that we have all run up against something beyond us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His rhetorical question burns with impatience. Should he wait while they stand mute? Or shall he fill the void? The vacuum of silence pulls at him. He is about to speak into a space that may not belong to him, answering a call that may not have been made.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I also will answer." The words tumble out now—his intention declared. He will have his say. There is a kind of energy here, almost feverish, as if words are a force he can no longer contain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Full of words. Constrained by spirit. This is the inner pressure before a voice breaks—the moment before confession, or before folly. The spirit within can be the Holy Spirit or our own burning certainty. We rarely know which until after we have spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wine with no vent; new wineskins ready to burst. Elihu uses the image of containment reaching its limit. A fermented word is powerful, dangerous, needing release. But a word spoken in pressure and haste often breaks things that should have remained whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He will speak to be refreshed. As if silence weighs him down and words will lighten the load. Sometimes speech brings clarity; sometimes it only moves the burden from one place to another. To speak without knowing which is to speak in darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He will not respect any man's person or give flattering titles. A promise of honesty, or a vow to let no earthly respect stop his tongue? Both, perhaps. He means to speak plainly, without the softening of deference. Yet sometimes deference and love are not so far apart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If he gave flattering titles, his Maker would take him away. Readers today hear an echo of this in the conscience that warns us against false words—the still voice reminding us that the Lord knows what is true in our hearts. Elihu fears his Maker's judgment as he speaks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
